modules.name: Atomic
modules.header:
Publishing a file under its final name without ever showing a reader a half-written one.
The rule every reliable writer follows: write the new contents somewhere else, force them to the device, then
move the finished file onto the final name in one step the filesystem cannot interrupt. A reader opening the
name at any moment sees the old file or the new one, never a truncated one and never a missing one — which is
what writing in place cannot promise, since a crash between truncating and finishing leaves exactly the
half-written file the whole exercise is meant to avoid.
Two details are not optional. The temporary must live in the **same directory** as the target, because a
rename is atomic only within a volume and a temporary directory is frequently on a different one — get that
wrong and the "atomic" publish silently becomes a copy-and-delete. And the contents must be synced **before**
the rename, not after: a rename that reaches the disk ahead of the data it names leaves the final name
pointing at a file whose contents never arrived.
What is not promised is that the directory entry itself survives a crash. That needs the containing directory
synced too, which needs a directory opened as a file — ordinary on the Unix systems, not a thing Windows
does. Rather than offer durability on one platform and pretend on another, this stops at the atomicity every
supported system gives, and says so.

modules.name: Directory
modules.header:
Directories: made, deleted, and read entry by entry with nothing lost in the names.
Enumeration hands back each entry's name as an `OsString` — the units the system actually stores, not a text
conversion that a hostile or merely foreign name would fail. The `.` and `..` entries are skipped, because no
caller walking a directory has ever wanted the directory itself twice. Order is whatever the filesystem
chooses; nothing here sorts, because a sorted walk is a policy and this is a primitive.

modules.name: File
modules.header:
An owned file handle, opened under options that say what they mean.
Opening a file asks two separate questions — what may happen through the handle, and what to do about the
file's existence — and most APIs tangle them. `OpenOptions` keeps them apart: `read`, `write` and `append`
answer the first; `create`, `createNew` and `truncate` answer the second. The contradictions are refused here,
before the platform is asked, so an impossible request fails the same way on every system instead of however
each platform happens to take it.
`File` owns its handle the way `String` owns its bytes: `Close` releases it exactly once and reports what the
platform said, and its destructor is the safety net that closes with the outcome discarded. A file being written
deserves the explicit `Close`, for the same reason a buffered writer deserves the explicit `Flush`: the
destructor has nowhere to report failure.

modules.name: FileStream
modules.header:
The open file as the streams everything else already speaks.
`File` implements `Reader`, `Writer` and `Seeker`, which is the whole point of those interfaces: the buffered
pair, line reading, binary values and format writing all stack on a file exactly as they stacked on memory and
the standard streams, none of them knowing the difference. Reads and writes are one attempt each, partial on
purpose — the looping belongs to `ReadExact` and `WriteAll`, written once for every stream.
`Flush` reports nothing gathered, because nothing is: these writes go to the platform as they are made. What a
caller usually wants after writing is `Sync`, which is a different promise — not "handed to the kernel" but
"acknowledged by the device", the one that holds through a power failure.

modules.name: Location
modules.header:
Where the process is, and what a path really refers to.
Two operations that look alike and are not. `Absolute` is arithmetic: it joins a relative path onto the
working directory and simplifies the result lexically, touching no filesystem and answering for a path that
does not exist. `Canonicalize` asks the filesystem: every symbolic link is resolved, every component must
exist, and the answer is the one true name of an existing file. `Path::Normalize` already documented that its
`x/..` simplification is a lie in the presence of symbolic links — this is where the truth lives, and the
difference between the two is the whole reason both are offered.
The working directory is process-wide state. Reading it is harmless; setting it reaches into every thread at
once and invalidates every relative path any of them was about to use, so `SetCurrentDirectory` exists for the
programs that genuinely need it and nothing in this package calls it.

modules.name: Metadata
modules.header:
What a file is, when it was touched, and who may do what to it.
The three systems disagree here more than anywhere else in this package, and the disagreement is reported
rather than papered over. Unix permissions are nine bits of owner/group/other; Windows has access-control
lists that the portable surface cannot express and one read-only attribute that it can. Rather than invent a
lowest common denominator and lie about it, `Permissions` carries both spellings, `Capabilities` says which
of them the running system actually honors, and a caller who cares can ask before it acts.
Timestamps are read on every system and written where the system allows it. Creation time is the one field
with no universal answer — Linux's `stat` does not carry it — so it arrives as a presence flag beside the
value rather than as a zero that pretends to be a date.

modules.name: Temporary
modules.header:
Temporary files and directories: unguessable names, and cleanup that is not left to chance.
The name comes from the entropy source rather than from a counter or the process id, because a predictable
name in a shared directory is the whole of the classic temp-file attack: an attacker who can guess the name
creates it first, as a symbolic link pointing somewhere it should not, and the program writes through it. The
name is also *claimed* rather than merely chosen — created with `createNew`, which fails rather than opens if
anything is already there — so winning the guess is not enough either. A collision is retried, since with 128
bits it means an attacker, not bad luck.
Cleanup is deterministic: the handle owns both the file and its name, and dropping it deletes both. That is
stronger than the platform conveniences it replaces — Windows' delete-on-close needs the last handle to go,
and the Unix trick of unlinking immediately leaves nothing a caller could pass to another process by name.

modules.name: Transfer
modules.header:
Moving file content and names around: copy, rename, and the two kinds of link.
The follow policies are stated rather than inherited. `CopyFile` follows a symbolic link and copies what it
points at, because copying the pointer would surprise every caller who asked for the bytes. `CreateHardLink`
does not follow: it links the name given, symbolic link and all, because a caller linking a link said so.
`DeleteFile` was already documented to remove the name, never the target. `Rename` moves the name whatever it
names, atomically within a volume, which is what makes it the publishing step of atomic replacement.

modules.name: Translate
modules.header:
What a platform failure means, translated in one place.
Every operating system reports failure as a small integer whose meaning lives in its own header files, and a
program that switches on those numbers at each call site rewrites this table badly, several times, in
disagreement with itself. So the table is written once per platform, and everything in this package reports
through it: an `IoError` whose kind is the meaning a caller acts on and whose raw field is the platform's own
code, preserved because the translation is honest about being lossy — many codes fold to `Other`, and the
number is how the rest stays diagnosable.

items.name: FileStream
items.signature: pub struct FileStream

doc.summary: A stored borrow of an open file that speaks the stream interfaces.
doc.markdown:
A stored borrow of an open file that speaks the stream interfaces.
**Reach for this only when a stream has to be kept.** A `File` already implements `Reader`, `Writer` and
`Seeker`, so anything taking one for the duration of a call takes the file itself:
```rux
let sink: &var Writer = file;
WriteAll(sink, contents);
```
That borrows, and the file is still the caller's afterwards. What it cannot do is outlive the call, because a
reference cannot be stored in a field — so a `BufferedReader`, which keeps its source, needs a value it can
hold. Binding the file itself into an interface value would move it, since a `File` owns its handle and
prohibits copying, and the caller would no longer have a file to close. This is the value that fills that gap:
it holds the file's address rather than the file, so it can be stored, and the file stays where it is.
The address is private, and `File::Stream` is the only way to obtain one. That is deliberate: a `FileStream`
assembled from an arbitrary pointer would be an unchecked promise about a file that may not exist, and the type
is already the least checkable thing in this package without adding a second way to get it wrong.
The file must outlive the stream, and must not be moved while one exists — a move relocates the file and
leaves the stored address pointing at where it used to be. Nothing here tracks either, which is exactly why
this is not the default way to reach a file's streams. A stream over a closed file is not unsafe: every
operation refuses with `InvalidHandle`, because the file itself checks.

fields.name: file
fields.doc: The file being borrowed. Private, so `File::Stream` is the only way to make one.

doc.summary: The one true name of the existing file `path` refers to.
doc.markdown:
The one true name of the existing file `path` refers to.
Every symbolic link is resolved, every `.` and `..` is applied against what those links actually mean, and
the result is absolute. Unlike `Absolute`, the file must exist: this is a question for the filesystem, and a
name with nothing behind it has no true form. A link chain that returns to itself is `LimitExceeded` rather
than a hang.
On Windows the answer arrives in the verbatim form and spelled as the filesystem stores it — the case the
name actually has, short names expanded — because that is what the system reports, and rewriting it would be
this package guessing.

doc.summary: Who may do what to a file, in both spellings the supported systems use.
doc.markdown:
Who may do what to a file, in both spellings the supported systems use.
`mode` is the Unix permission bits, the low nine of which are the owner/group/other triple. `readOnly` is
Windows' one portable attribute. Both are always filled: on Windows the mode is synthesized from the
attribute (`0o444` when read-only, `0o666` otherwise) so a program that reasons in Unix terms is not blocked,
and on Unix `readOnly` reports whether the owner-write bit is clear. `Capabilities` says which one is real.

doc.summary: Everything a single query can say about a file.
doc.markdown: Everything a single query can say about a file.

fields.name: kind
fields.doc: What the name refers to.

fields.name: size
fields.doc: The length in bytes; zero for a directory, whose size means nothing portable.

fields.name: linkCount
fields.doc: How many names the content has. Always one on a system that does not count them.

fields.name: permissions
fields.doc: Who may do what.

fields.name: accessed
fields.doc: When the contents were last read.

fields.name: modified
fields.doc: When the contents were last written.

fields.name: created
fields.doc: When the file came into being, where the system records that.

fields.name: hasCreated
fields.doc: Whether `created` means anything.

items.name: Capabilities
items.signature: pub struct Capabilities

doc.summary: What the running system can actually answer, so a caller can ask before it assumes.
doc.markdown: What the running system can actually answer, so a caller can ask before it assumes.

fields.name: unixPermissions
fields.doc: Whether `Permissions::mode` is the system's own answer rather than one synthesized from a flag.

fields.name: creationTime
fields.doc: Whether the system records a creation time.

fields.name: hardLinkCounts
fields.doc: Whether names have a meaningful link count.

fields.name: settableTimes
fields.doc: Whether setting timestamps is supported at all.

items.name: CapabilitiesOfSystem
items.signature: pub func CapabilitiesOfSystem() -> Capabilities

doc.summary: What this system can answer.
doc.markdown: What this system can answer.
doc.returns: what this system's metadata actually carries, so a caller can tell an absent value from a false one

items.name: MetadataOf
items.signature: pub func MetadataOf(allocator: Allocator, path: Path, followLinks: bool) -> Metadata ! IoError

doc.summary: Describes the file `path` names.
doc.markdown:
Describes the file `path` names.
`followLinks` decides what a symbolic link at the end of the path means: following it describes the target,
and not following it describes the link, which is the only way `SymbolicLink` is ever reported.

params.name: followLinks
params.markdown: whether a final symbolic link is followed rather than described

doc.returns: what the system knows about the path

items.name: SetPermissions
items.signature: pub func SetPermissions(allocator: Allocator, path: Path, permissions: Permissions) -> ! IoError

doc.summary: Sets who may do what to the file `path` names.
doc.markdown:
Sets who may do what to the file `path` names.
On the Unix systems the mode bits are written as given. On Windows only the read-only attribute exists, so
that alone is written and the rest of `permissions` is ignored — ask `CapabilitiesOfSystem` first if the
difference matters. A symbolic link is always followed: its own bits mean nothing on any supported system.
doc.returns: success when the permissions were applied

items.name: SetTimes
items.signature: pub func SetTimes(allocator: Allocator, path: Path, accessed: Timestamp, modified: Timestamp, followLinks: bool) -> ! IoError

doc.summary: Sets the access and modification times of the file `path` names.
doc.markdown:
Sets the access and modification times of the file `path` names.
Creation time is not settable here: Windows would allow it and the Unix systems would not, and an operation
that silently means different things on different systems is worse than one that is not offered.

params.name: accessed
params.markdown: the access time to set, or `None` to leave it

params.name: modified
params.markdown: the modification time to set, or `None` to leave it

params.name: followLinks
params.markdown: whether a final symbolic link is followed rather than described

doc.returns: success when the times were applied

items.name: TemporaryNameAttempts
items.signature: pub const TemporaryNameAttempts: uint

doc.summary: How many names are tried before a temporary file gives up.
doc.markdown:
How many names are tried before a temporary file gives up.
With 128 bits of name, one collision is already a surprise and three in a row is not chance; failing is the
honest response to an entropy source that has stopped being one.

items.name: TemporaryDirectory
items.signature: pub func TemporaryDirectory(allocator: Allocator) -> PathBuffer ! IoError

doc.summary: The directory the system sets aside for temporary files.
doc.markdown:
The directory the system sets aside for temporary files.
On Windows this is what the platform reports, which consults `TMP`, `TEMP` and `USERPROFILE` in turn. On the
Unix systems it is `/tmp`: reading `TMPDIR` needs environment access this package does not have yet, so a
caller who must honor it passes the directory to the functions below instead.
doc.returns: the system's directory for temporary files

items.name: TemporaryFile
items.signature: pub struct TemporaryFile

doc.summary: A temporary file that owns both its contents and its name.
doc.markdown:
A temporary file that owns both its contents and its name.
Move-only. `Close` deletes the file and reports what the deletion said; destruction does the same with the outcome
discarded. `Keep` gives up ownership of the name instead, for the caller who has decided the file should
outlive this value — which is what a rename into place is built on.

fields.name: file
fields.doc: The open file.

fields.name: path
fields.doc: Its full path.

fields.name: owned
fields.doc: Whether the name is still this value's to delete.

members.name: Create
members.signature: pub func Create(allocator: Allocator, directory: Path, prefix: char8[..]) -> TemporaryFile ! IoError

doc.summary: Creates a new temporary file in `directory`, named from `prefix` and sixteen hex digits of entropy.
doc.markdown:
Creates a new temporary file in `directory`, named from `prefix` and sixteen hex digits of entropy.
The file is opened for reading and writing and is created, never opened: a name that already exists is a
collision, and the next name is tried.

params.name: directory
params.markdown: the directory to create it in

params.name: prefix
params.markdown: the text the generated name starts with

doc.returns: the created file, which is removed when closed unless kept

doc.summary: The file's path, for handing to something that needs a name.
doc.markdown: The file's path, for handing to something that needs a name.
doc.returns: the path it was created at

members.name: Close
members.signature: pub func Close(self: &var TemporaryFile, allocator: Allocator) -> ! IoError

doc.summary: Closes the file and deletes it, reporting the first thing that went wrong.
doc.markdown: Closes the file and deletes it, reporting the first thing that went wrong.
doc.returns: success when it was removed

doc.summary: Closes the file and leaves it where it is, giving up the name.
doc.markdown: Closes the file and leaves it where it is, giving up the name.
doc.returns: success when it will be left in place rather than removed

doc.summary: Closes and deletes with the outcome discarded: the safety net, not the contract.
doc.markdown:
Closes and deletes with the outcome discarded: the safety net, not the contract.
A destructor has nowhere to report a failed deletion, so a caller who needs to know calls `Close`. What
this guarantees is that a temporary file is never left behind by an early return or a failure path, which
is the reason the type exists.

items.name: TemporaryDirectoryHandle
items.signature: pub struct TemporaryDirectoryHandle

doc.summary: A temporary directory that owns its name.
doc.markdown:
A temporary directory that owns its name.
Move-only, with the same contract as `TemporaryFile`: `Close` removes it and reports, destruction removes it
quietly, `Keep` gives up ownership. Removal is of the directory itself and requires it to be empty — nothing
here deletes a tree, because a temporary directory that silently erased whatever a caller put inside it
would be a worse surprise than a refusal.

fields.name: path
fields.doc: The directory's full path.

fields.name: owned
fields.doc: Whether the name is still this value's to remove.

members.name: Create
members.signature: pub func Create(allocator: Allocator, directory: Path, prefix: char8[..]) -> TemporaryDirectoryHandle ! IoError

doc.summary: Creates a new temporary directory in `directory`, named from `prefix` and sixteen hex digits of entropy.
doc.markdown: Creates a new temporary directory in `directory`, named from `prefix` and sixteen hex digits of entropy.

params.name: directory
params.markdown: the directory to create it in

params.name: prefix
params.markdown: the text the generated name starts with

doc.returns: the created directory, which is removed when closed unless kept

doc.summary: The directory's path, for building names inside it.
doc.markdown: The directory's path, for building names inside it.
doc.returns: the path it was created at

members.name: Close
members.signature: pub func Close(self: &var TemporaryDirectoryHandle, allocator: Allocator) -> ! IoError

doc.summary: Removes the directory and reports what the removal said.
doc.markdown: Removes the directory and reports what the removal said.
doc.returns: success when it was removed

doc.summary: Leaves the directory where it is, giving up the name.
doc.markdown: Leaves the directory where it is, giving up the name.

doc.summary: Removes the directory with the outcome discarded: the safety net, not the contract.
doc.markdown: Removes the directory with the outcome discarded: the safety net, not the contract.

items.name: Rename
items.signature: pub func Rename(allocator: Allocator, from: Path, to: Path) -> ! IoError

doc.summary: Renames `from` to `to`, moving it between directories if the paths differ there.
doc.markdown:
Renames `from` to `to`, moving it between directories if the paths differ there.
An existing `to` is replaced, atomically within one volume: a reader sees the old file or the new, never a
gap. Across volumes Windows copies and deletes instead — not atomic — and the Unix systems refuse.

params.name: to
params.markdown: the path it should have afterwards

doc.returns: success when the file is at its new path

items.name: CreateHardLink
items.signature: pub func CreateHardLink(allocator: Allocator, existing: Path, link: Path) -> ! IoError

doc.summary: Creates `link` as a hard link: a second name for the file `existing` names.
doc.markdown:
Creates `link` as a hard link: a second name for the file `existing` names.
The two names are then equals — neither is "the original" — and the content lives until the last name is
deleted. A symbolic link at `existing` is not followed: the link is made to the name given. Directories
cannot be hard-linked on any supported system.
doc.returns: success when the new name refers to the same file

items.name: CreateSymbolicLink
items.signature: pub func CreateSymbolicLink(allocator: Allocator, target: Path, link: Path, targetIsDirectory: bool) -> ! IoError

doc.summary: Creates `link` as a symbolic link holding `target` as its text.
doc.markdown:
Creates `link` as a symbolic link holding `target` as its text.
The target is stored, not checked: a dangling link is created as readily as a good one. `targetIsDirectory`
matters only on Windows, which types its links; the Unix systems ignore it. Windows also gates creation
behind a privilege unless the machine runs Developer Mode, so `PermissionDenied` here is an environment, not
a bug.

params.name: target
params.markdown: the path the link will point at, which need not exist

params.name: targetIsDirectory
params.markdown: whether the target is a directory, which Windows must be told in advance

doc.returns: success when the link was created; Windows needs a privilege for this

items.name: CopyFile
items.signature: pub func CopyFile(allocator: Allocator, from: Path, to: Path) -> ! IoError

doc.summary: Copies the file `from` names to `to`, following a symbolic link to the bytes it points at.
doc.markdown:
Copies the file `from` names to `to`, following a symbolic link to the bytes it points at.
An existing `to` is replaced. The copy is the bytes and nothing else: permissions, timestamps and the rest of
the metadata are the destination's own, fresh — carrying them is a policy the metadata work owns.

params.name: to
params.markdown: the path it should have afterwards

doc.returns: success when the destination holds a copy

items.name: NativeKind
items.signature: pub func NativeKind(raw: int32) -> IoErrorKind

doc.summary: The meaning of a platform error code on the platform this program was compiled for.
doc.markdown:
The meaning of a platform error code on the platform this program was compiled for.
Codes with no portable meaning translate to `Other`; the caller still has the raw code beside it.

params.name: raw
params.markdown: the platform's own error number or code

doc.returns: the kind this package gives that platform code

items.signature: pub func TranslateNative(raw: int32) -> IoError

doc.summary: A platform error code as the structured error everything here reports.
doc.markdown: A platform error code as the structured error everything here reports.

params.name: raw
params.markdown: the platform's own error number or code

doc.returns: the error this package gives that platform code, keeping the raw value
